## Introduction

Reproduction of BTC-S&P500 correlation analysis using GARCH model family
(GARCH, EGARCH, GJR-GARCH, APARCH) and DCC-GARCH for time-varying correlation.
Extended with Oil, Gold and the VIX volatility index.

## Data

We reproduce the original Kaggle dataset and extend it with additional
assets pulled from Yahoo Finance. Both are daily log-returns.

### Replication dataset (Kaggle)

BTC and S&P 500, recomputed from the original CSV (2011-2022).

```{python}
from garch_btc_sp.data.preprocessing import build_kaggle_returns
from garch_btc_sp.stats.descriptive import descriptive_stats

kaggle = build_kaggle_returns()
descriptive_stats(kaggle)
```

### Extended dataset (Yahoo Finance)

BTC and S&P 500 plus Oil, Gold and the VIX volatility index. Pre-computed
log-returns loaded from the processed data baked into the image.

```{python}
import pandas as pd

yahoo = pd.read_parquet("data/processed/returns_yahoo.parquet")
descriptive_stats(yahoo)
```

## Diagnostic Tests

ADF (stationarity), Jarque-Bera (normality), Ljung-Box on returns and their
squares, and Engle's ARCH-LM test, run per asset. Low ARCH-LM p-values
confirm conditional heteroskedasticity and justify GARCH-family modelling.

### Replication dataset (Kaggle)

```{python}
from garch_btc_sp.stats.tests import run_all_tests

run_all_tests(kaggle)
```

### Extended dataset (Yahoo Finance)

```{python}
run_all_tests(yahoo)
```

## Univariate GARCH Models

Four GARCH-family variants (GARCH, EGARCH, GJR-GARCH, APARCH) are each fitted
with three error distributions (normal, Student-t, skewed-t) to BTC and the
S&P 500. Models are compared by AIC/BIC and Ljung-Box p-values on the
standardized residuals (and their squares); the best model per asset is chosen
by BIC.

```{python}
from garch_btc_sp.models import fit_model_grid, compare_models, select_best_by_bic

garch_assets = ["BTC", "SP500"]
grids = {asset: fit_model_grid(yahoo[asset]) for asset in garch_assets}
comparison = compare_models([m for models in grids.values() for m in models])
comparison
```

Best model per asset (lowest BIC):

```{python}
best = select_best_by_bic(comparison)
best
```

Conditional volatility of the selected models:

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(len(garch_assets), 1, figsize=(9, 6), sharex=True)
for ax, asset in zip(axes, garch_assets):
    row = best[best["asset"] == asset].iloc[0]
    model = next(
        m for m in grids[asset]
        if m.variant == row["model"] and m.distribution == row["distribution"]
    )
    model.conditional_volatility.plot(ax=ax)
    ax.set_title(f"{asset}: {row['model']} ({row['distribution']}) conditional volatility")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## DCC-GARCH - Time-Varying Correlation

The Dynamic Conditional Correlation model (Engle, 2002) is estimated in two
steps: the standardized residuals of the BIC-selected univariate GARCH models
feed a DCC(1,1) recursion, yielding a time-varying correlation between BTC and
the S&P 500 rather than a single static coefficient.

```{python}
from garch_btc_sp.models.dcc import DCCModel
from garch_btc_sp.visualization import plot_time_varying_correlation


def _best_model(asset):
    row = best[best["asset"] == asset].iloc[0]
    return next(
        m for m in grids[asset]
        if m.variant == row["model"] and m.distribution == row["distribution"]
    )


std_resid = pd.DataFrame(
    {asset: _best_model(asset).standardized_residuals for asset in garch_assets}
).dropna()

dcc = DCCModel(std_resid).fit()
dcc.summary()
```

Estimated DCC dynamics (time-varying BTC–S&P 500 correlation):

```{python}
plot_time_varying_correlation(dcc, "BTC", "SP500")
```

## Comparison with the Original Study

```{python}
_s = dcc.summary()
_corr = dcc.get_correlation("BTC", "SP500")
mean_corr = round(float(_corr.mean()), 2)
min_corr = round(float(_corr.min()), 2)
max_corr = round(float(_corr.max()), 2)
persistence = round(float(_s["alpha_plus_beta"]), 3)
_btc = best[best["asset"] == "BTC"].iloc[0]
_sp = best[best["asset"] == "SP500"].iloc[0]
btc_model = f"{_btc['model']} / {_btc['distribution']}"
sp_model = f"{_sp['model']} / {_sp['distribution']}"
```

The original analysis is a Kaggle notebook (*linhanphm*, written in R with
`rugarch`) titled "The Hedging and Diversification Abilities of Bitcoin Against
the Stock Market". The table below contrasts its design and findings with this
reproduction.

| Dimension | Original (linhanphm, R) | This project (Python) |
|---|---|---|
| Sample | BTC + S&P 500, Jan 2011 – Dec 2022 | Replication 2011–2022, extended with Oil, Gold, VIX (Yahoo, 2014–present) |
| Volatility models | GARCH, EGARCH, GJR — **normal** errors only | GARCH, EGARCH, GJR, APARCH × normal / Student-t / skewed-t |
| Model selection | All three reported; AIC/BIC roughly tied (GARCH ≈ GJR) | BIC selects `{python} btc_model` (BTC), `{python} sp_model` (S&P 500) |
| Correlation measure | **Static** — S&P coefficient β₂ in the BTC mean equation | **Dynamic** — DCC-GARCH(1,1) conditional correlation |
| BTC–S&P result | Positive, significant (β₂ ≈ 0.74–0.76) | Positive on average (`{python} mean_corr`), ranging `{python} min_corr` to `{python} max_corr` |
| Leverage effect | Present but mild (EGARCH α<0, GJR γ>0) | Captured via the asymmetric APARCH spec chosen by BIC |
| Reproducibility | Single Kaggle R notebook | Docker + Quarto + Sphinx, one-command rebuild |

**Where the results agree.** Both studies reach the same headline: Bitcoin is
*positively* associated with the S&P 500 and therefore behaves as a diversifier
rather than a hedge (in the Baur–Lucey sense). Both detect volatility
asymmetry — the original through a negative EGARCH α and positive GJR γ, ours
through BIC preferring the asymmetric APARCH model — and both confirm strong
ARCH effects that justify GARCH modelling in the first place.

**Where they differ.** The central methodological gap is the correlation
itself. Despite its framing, the original never estimates a time-varying
correlation: it reads "correlation" off the contemporaneous S&P regressor
β₂ ≈ 0.75 and treats it as constant across 2011–2022. That coefficient is a
return *sensitivity*, not a conditional correlation, so it is not directly
comparable to our average DCC correlation of `{python} mean_corr`. The DCC,
which the paper's title implies but never implements, shows the relationship is
**not** constant — it ranges from `{python} min_corr` to `{python} max_corr`
and is highly persistent (α + β = `{python} persistence`), tightening in
stress periods. This nuances the original's blanket "diversifier" claim:
diversification weakens precisely when it is most needed. We also relax the
original's normal-error assumption — which its own goodness-of-fit tests
reject — and BIC selects skewed-t, and we broaden the asset set beyond the
single BTC–S&P pair.

## Conclusions

This study reproduced the Kaggle BTC–S&P 500 correlation analysis and extended
it with Oil, Gold and the VIX pulled from Yahoo Finance. The diagnostic tests
confirm the stylized facts that motivate GARCH modelling: returns are heavily
non-normal (Jarque-Bera) and exhibit strong conditional heteroskedasticity
(significant ARCH-LM and Ljung-Box statistics on squared returns), so a
constant-variance model is inadequate.

At the univariate stage, BIC selects an asymmetric, fat-tailed specification
for each series — `{python} btc_model` for BTC and `{python} sp_model` for the
S&P 500 — consistent with the leverage effect and heavy tails documented in the
literature. These fitted models supply the standardized residuals that drive
the second stage.

The central result is the **Dynamic Conditional Correlation**. The BTC–S&P 500
correlation is not a single number: it averages `{python} mean_corr` but ranges
from `{python} min_corr` to `{python} max_corr` across the sample, so the
relationship is regime-dependent rather than constant. The estimated DCC
persistence (α + β = `{python} persistence`) is close to unity, meaning shocks
to the correlation decay slowly — periods of high co-movement, such as broad
market stress, persist rather than reverting immediately. This qualifies the
common claim that Bitcoin is a reliable equity diversifier: its co-movement with
the S&P 500 tightens precisely when diversification would be most valuable.

The whole pipeline is reproducible end-to-end: the dataset is baked into a
Docker image, `make report` regenerates this document, and `make docs` builds
the Sphinx API reference from the package docstrings. The natural extension is a
full multivariate DCC across all five assets (adding Oil, Gold and the VIX) to
map how Bitcoin's hedging properties vary against several markets at once.
